questions.question: On a technically adequate MLO (Mediolateral Oblique) view, the pectoralis muscle should be visualized down to what level?
choices: The level of the inframammary fold
It does not need to be visualized
questions.detail: Visualizing the pectoralis to the nipple level ensures that the deep posterior breast tissue is included in the image.

questions.question: The 'Posterior Nipple Line' (PNL) measured on the CC and MLO views should be within how many centimeters of each other to ensure adequate positioning?
questions.detail: A difference greater than 1 cm suggests that one of the views (usually the CC) has excluded a significant amount of posterior tissue.

questions.question: When localizing a lesion seen on both CC and MLO views, if the lesion moves CEPHALAD (up) on the MLO view compared to its position on a true lateral view, it is located in the:
questions.detail: The mnemonic 'Muffins Rise' (Medial Rises) describes how medial lesions appear higher on the MLO, while lateral lesions ('Lead Sinks') appear lower.

questions.question: Which mammographic view is specifically used to better image tissue in the 'far lateral' aspect of the breast?
questions.detail: The XCCL is a modified CC view where the patient is rotated to include the axillary tail and far lateral parenchyma.

questions.question: A 'Rolled CC' view is typically performed to:
choices: Confirm a finding is real versus a summation artifact
Localize a lesion seen only on the CC view
questions.detail: Rolling the breast tissue allows the radiologist to see if an asymmetry persists or moves, helping to triangulate lesions seen in only one projection.

questions.question: According to the Mammography Quality Standards Act (MQSA), what is the maximum allowable 'Average Glandular Dose' per view for a standard breast phantom?
questions.detail: This dose limit is strictly regulated to ensure patient safety while maintaining image quality.

questions.question: Magnification mammography requires the use of a smaller focal spot size to minimize geometric blur. What is the standard focal spot size used?
questions.detail: Standard contact mammography uses a 0.3 mm focal spot, while magnification requires 0.1 mm for higher resolution.

questions.question: Why is a 'grid' typically NOT used during magnification mammography?
choices: It increases the radiation dose too much
An air gap is introduced which naturally reduces scatter
Grids are only used for thick breasts
questions.detail: The increased object-to-detector distance (air gap) allows scattered photons to miss the detector, making a grid unnecessary and allowing for lower mAs.

questions.question: An 'architectural distortion' on mammography is defined as:
choices: Thin lines radiating from a point without an associated discrete mass
questions.detail: Architectural distortion is a highly suspicious finding (often BI-RADS 4) that may represent malignancy or a radial scar.

questions.question: Which type of calcification distribution is considered the MOST suspicious for malignancy?
questions.detail: These distributions suggest that the calcifications are following the path of a duct, a hallmark of DCIS.

questions.question: 'Fine pleomorphic' calcifications are characterized by:
choices: Small, irregular shapes with varying sizes and shapes (shards of glass)
questions.detail: Fine pleomorphic calcifications are higher-probability suspicious findings compared to amorphous or coarse heterogeneous ones.

questions.question: 'Popcorn' calcifications are pathognomonic for which benign entity?
questions.detail: As fibroadenomas involute in postmenopausal women, they develop characteristic large, coarse, 'popcorn' calcifications.

questions.question: 'Milk of calcium' calcifications are best identified by which mammographic feature?
choices: Changing shape from 'smudgy' on the CC to 'crescentic' or 'tea-cupped' on a 90-degree lateral view
Being located exclusively in the skin
questions.detail: These represent sedimented calcium in small cysts; the horizontal x-ray beam of a lateral view demonstrates the 'fluid-calcium' level.

questions.question: Secretory (Plasma Cell Mastitis) calcifications are characterized by:
choices: Large, solid, 'cigar-shaped' rods that point toward the nipple
Tiny clusters in a segmental distribution
questions.detail: These are benign (BI-RADS 2) calcifications resulting from ductal secretions.

questions.question: A 'Global Asymmetry' is defined as involving at least what percentage of the breast?
questions.detail: Global asymmetries are often normal variants but require comparison with the contralateral breast.

questions.question: A 'Focal Asymmetry' differs from a mass because it:
choices: Is only seen on one view
Lacks outward-convex borders and a discrete center
questions.detail: Unlike a mass, a focal asymmetry does not have a three-dimensional shape that displaces normal tissue.

questions.question: If a suspicious mass is seen on only the MLO view and NOT the CC view, what is the next best step for triangulation?
choices: Repeat the CC view with more compression
questions.detail: The lateral view helps determine the true height and position to see if the lesion was 'rising' or 'sinking'.

questions.question: 'Oil cysts' and 'eggshell' calcifications are typically the end result of:
questions.detail: Following trauma or surgery, damaged fat can liquefy and subsequently calcify peripherally, forming an oil cyst.

questions.question: To meet MQSA requirements, an interpreting physician must have read how many mammograms during the last 24 months of their training?
questions.detail: These 240 mammograms must be read during a 6-month period within those last 24 months of training.

questions.question: 'Tangential' mammographic views are specifically helpful for:
choices: Confirming that a finding is located within the skin
questions.detail: By placing a lead marker over a lesion and turning the breast profile, skin lesions will be seen directly under the marker.

questions.question: Which mammographic finding is most suggestive of an 'Invasive Lobular Carcinoma' (ILC), which is notoriously difficult to detect?
choices: Subtle architectural distortion or a shrinking breast on serial films
questions.detail: ILC cells often grow in 'single files' that do not form a discrete mass, making architectural distortion a key clue.

questions.question: 'Ductography' (Galactography) is an interventional technique used to evaluate:
questions.detail: Contrast is injected into the discharging duct to identify intraductal masses like papillomas or DCIS.

questions.question: A 'Cleavage View' (CV) is designed to image:
choices: The far medial aspect of both breasts simultaneously
questions.detail: This view (also called 'Double Breast' view) captures tissue that might be missed on standard CC views.

questions.question: A mammographic mass described as 'Round' with 'Spiculated' margins should be assigned which preliminary BI-RADS category?
questions.detail: Spiculated margins are highly suspicious for malignancy and require tissue sampling.

questions.question: Which feature of a mass is considered MOST reliable for benignity on mammography?
choices: Location in the upper outer quadrant
questions.detail: Masses containing fat (e.g., lymph nodes, hamartomas, lipomas, or oil cysts) are almost always benign.
